propositions.text: This appeal arises from the Federal Court dismissing the appellant's judicial review and mandamus applications.
propositions.quote: This appeal arises from a decision of the Federal Court ... dismissing the appellant’s application for judicial review ... The Federal Court also dismissed the appellant’s application for mandamus

propositions.text: The Federal Court found the judicial review did not challenge a matter within section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act.
propositions.quote: ... as it did not challenge a matter within the scope of section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act

propositions.text: The Federal Court found the appellant failed to identify a public legal duty to act by the RCMP Commissioner for mandamus.
propositions.quote: ... the appellant failed to identify a public legal duty to act on the part of the respondent Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) Commissioner.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the appeal arises from the Federal Court dismissing the appellant's judicial review and mandamus applications for lack of jurisdiction and public legal duty.

propositions.text: The Federal Court Decision set out the facts but found the appellant's affidavits disjointed and difficult to chronologically piece together.
propositions.quote: The judge observed that it was “difficult to piece together a chronology of events” given the appellant’s “disjointed affidavits ...

propositions.text: The appellant's sister and brother-in-law were involved in lengthy family law proceedings in Alberta.
propositions.quote: ... the appellant’s sister and then brother-in-law became embroiled in lengthy divorce, custody, and access proceedings in the Alberta Court of King’s Bench.

propositions.text: The appellant’s sister made domestic and child abuse allegations against her husband to the RCMP.
propositions.quote: The appellant’s sister subsequently made allegations of domestic and child abuse against her then husband to the RCMP.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Federal Court found the appellant's affidavits disjointed and that the appellant's sister made abuse allegations to the RCMP during family law proceedings.

propositions.text: In February 2021, the appellant filed two complaints to the CRCC requesting investigation of RCMP conduct regarding her sister's allegations.
propositions.quote: In February 2021, the appellant filed two complaints to the Civilian Review and Complaints Commission for the RCMP (CRCC) requesting that it investigate the RCMP’s conduct ...

propositions.text: Under the RCMP Act, individuals may complain about RCMP member conduct in performing duties.
propositions.quote: Under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act ... an individual may make a complaint concerning the conduct of a member of the RCMP in the performance of a duty or function (RCMP Act, s. 45.53(1)).

propositions.text: The CRCC's mandate and procedures are described in British Columbia Civil Liberties Association v. Canada (RCMP).
propositions.quote: A review of the mandate and procedures of the CRCC can be found in British Columbia Civil Liberties Association v. Canada (Royal Mounted Police), 2021 FC 1475 at paras. 7-8, per Gagné, A.C.J.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant filed complaints to the CRCC about RCMP conduct, explains the RCMP Act complaint process, and references CRCC mandate case law.

propositions.text: The appellant requested the CRCC address management and conduct issues in two RCMP detachments, which was beyond CRCC jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: The appellant also requested the CRCC address “the overall management and conduct of the Cochrane and Airdrie detachments ...” The CRCC did not address this issue as it was beyond its jurisdiction ...

propositions.text: The CRCC referred the management issue to the RCMP Commissioner, who delegated it to the OISP for internal review.
propositions.quote: This allegation was then directed to the RCMP’s Office of Investigative Standards and Practices (OISP) for an internal administrative review.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the appellant's management complaints were outside CRCC jurisdiction and referred to the RCMP Commissioner and OISP for internal review.

propositions.text: In April to June 2023, the appellant emailed the Commissioner requesting disclosure of the OISP review and confirmation of disclosure in family law proceedings.
propositions.quote: In April, May and June 2023, the appellant sent the Commissioner several emails, requesting disclosure of the OISP review. In an email dated May 26, the appellant requested confirmation ...

propositions.text: On June 19, the appellant requested responses to 20 questions about the OISP review of detachment mismanagement.
propositions.quote: In a June 19th email the appellant requested “response and clarification” to 20 questions the appellant had concerning the OISP review ...

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant emailed the Commissioner in 2023 seeking disclosure of the OISP review and answers to 20 questions about detachment mismanagement.

propositions.text: The June 19 email set a June 23 deadline for response, threatening to treat non-response as a reviewable decision.
propositions.quote: The June 19th email set a deadline for response of June 23, 2023, failing which the appellant would consider the RCMP's lack of response to be a reviewable decision.

propositions.text: The June 19 email described the decision as the RCMP Commissioner choosing not to address ongoing conduct related to the complaint.
propositions.quote: The June 19th email described the decision as follows: [...] as of June 19, 2023, the RCMP Commissioner and/or the RCMP have made the reviewable decision to not address the ongoing conduct of the RCMP relating to my [Public Complaint] ...

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the appellant's June 19 email set a response deadline and described the RCMP's non-response as a reviewable decision.

propositions.text: The Department of Justice responded on behalf of the Commissioner seeking clarification of the appellant's request and counsel status in family proceedings.
propositions.quote: The Department of Justice responded to the June 19th email on behalf of the Commissioner. Counsel sought clarification of the appellant’s request as well as confirmation whether she had been retained as counsel ...

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Department of Justice responded on behalf of the Commissioner seeking clarification of the appellant's request and counsel status.

propositions.text: Shortly after the Department of Justice response, the appellant filed the judicial review application before Lafrenière J.
propositions.quote: Shortly thereafter, the appellant filed the judicial review application that came before Lafrenière J.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the appellant filed the judicial review application shortly after the Department of Justice's response.

propositions.text: The Federal Court judge noted the relief sought was narrowed to a declaration of breach, setting aside the decision, and mandamus to investigate misconduct and mismanagement.
propositions.quote: In his reasons for judgment dismissing the application, the judge noted (at para. 21) that the broad relief sought ... had been whittled down ... to a declaration that the Commissioner breached his duty ... an order setting aside the alleged decision, and an order for mandamus ...

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge found the relief sought was narrowed to breach declaration, setting aside decision, and mandamus to investigate misconduct.

propositions.text: Jurisdictional questions about 'matter' under section 18.1(1) of the Federal Courts Act are reviewed on a correctness standard.
propositions.quote: Questions as to what constitutes a “matter” within subsection 18.1(1) of the Federal Courts Act go to the jurisdiction of the Court and are assessed on the standard of correctness ...

propositions.text: Mandamus's first criterion, public legal duty, is reviewed on correctness; other criteria on palpable and overriding error.
propositions.quote: Similarly, the first criterion for mandamus, namely whether there is a public legal duty, is assessed on a correctness basis, with the balance of the mandamus criteria raising questions of mixed fact and law reviewable on a standard of palpable and overriding error ...

paragraphs.summary: The court states jurisdictional questions and mandamus public legal duty are reviewed on correctness; other mandamus criteria on palpable and overriding error.

propositions.text: The court finds no error in the Federal Court's reasons.
propositions.quote: I see no error in the reasons of the Federal Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in the Federal Court's reasons.

propositions.text: A matter not affecting legal rights, obligations, or prejudicial effects is not reviewable.
propositions.quote: a matter that fails to affect legal rights, impose legal obligations, or cause prejudicial effects is not reviewable ...

propositions.text: The Commissioner's lack of response to the June 19 email was not a reviewable decision as it did not affect legal rights, duties, or cause prejudice.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner’s lack of response to the appellant’s June 19th email did not constitute a reviewable decision as it did not affect the appellant’s legal rights, impose legal obligations, or have prejudicial effects.

propositions.text: The appellant had no legal right to answers, the Commissioner had no legal duty to respond, and non-response had no prejudicial effect.
propositions.quote: The appellant had no legal right to be provided with answers to her questions, the Commissioner had no legal duty or obligation to respond to the appellant’s questions, and the non-response did not have prejudicial effects.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court found the Commissioner's non-response was not reviewable as it did not affect legal rights, duties, or cause prejudice.

propositions.text: The Commissioner had no legal duty to conduct the OISP internal review, nor did its results affect the appellant's legal rights.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner was under no legal duty to conduct an internal review of the allegations, nor do the results of that review, if any, affect the appellant’s legal rights.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court found no legal duty to conduct the OISP review and no effect on appellant's legal rights from it.

propositions.text: The appellant argues judicial review is essential to hold the RCMP accountable for misleading the Alberta Court of King’s Bench.
propositions.quote: The appellant places considerable emphasis on the importance of judicial review to ensure that public officers conduct themselves according to law and argues that judicial review is the only way in which the RCMP can be held accountable for what she says was misleading the Alberta Court of King’s Bench.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues judicial review is necessary to hold the RCMP accountable for misleading the Alberta Court of King’s Bench.

propositions.text: The court finds the appellant's argument parallels Democracy Watch 2009, where failure to investigate did not affect rights or impose duty.
propositions.quote: This argument parallels that made by the appellant in Democracy Watch, 2009 ... The argument was rejected by this Court which concluded that the Ethics Commissioner had no duty to investigate beyond that prescribed by statute.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant's argument parallels Democracy Watch 2009, where failure to investigate was not a duty or rights violation.

propositions.text: Parliament creates formal complaints procedures with express duties on public officers to investigate.
propositions.quote: Where Parliament creates a formal complaints procedure with a concomitant duty on an agent of Parliament or public officer to investigate, it does so expressly ...

propositions.text: Parliament did not create a general complaints procedure imposing a legal obligation on the Commissioner beyond statutory requirements.
propositions.quote: In establishing the CRCC process, Parliament did not create a general complaints procedure that gave rise to a legal obligation on the Commissioner to respond to demands beyond the scope of what is required by statute ...

propositions.text: By statute, the appellant had the right to file a complaint, have it investigated, and receive a response, which she has.
propositions.quote: By statute, the appellant had a right to file a complaint, to have it investigated and to receive a response, which she now has.

propositions.text: The question of the appellant's standing to file a complaint was not raised before the court.
propositions.quote: I note, parenthetically, that the question whether the appellant, who was neither the spouse nor the mother at the center of the domestic and child abuse allegations, had standing to file a complaint was not raised before us.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament did not impose a legal duty on the Commissioner beyond statute; the appellant had complaint rights and standing was not challenged.

propositions.text: The RCMP delivered a detailed report on the appellant's 14 allegations on January 25, 2024, concluding the investigation was complete.
propositions.quote: The RCMP delivered its report on the two complaints on January 25, 2024. It addressed each of the appellant’s 14 allegations in considerable detail. The report concluded: Please be advised that pursuant to section 45.64 of the RCMP Act, I am notifying you that the investigation into this complaint has now been concluded.

propositions.text: The report advised the appellant of her right to request a CRCC review within 60 days if dissatisfied.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, according to section 45.7(1), if you are not satisfied with the manner in which your complaint has been disposed by the RCMP, you may request a review by the CRCC by writing to them within 60 days ...

paragraphs.summary: The court states the RCMP delivered a detailed report concluding the investigation and advised the appellant of her right to request CRCC review.

propositions.text: The court turns to consider the appellant's request for an order of mandamus.
propositions.quote: I turn next to the request for an order of mandamus.

paragraphs.summary: The court proceeds to consider the appellant's mandamus request.

propositions.text: The Federal Court concluded the appellant did not meet the mandamus test requiring a public legal duty and clear right to performance.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court concluded that the appellant did not meet the test for mandamus set out in Apotex. That test requires the appellant establish, inter alia, that the Commissioner owed her a public legal duty to act, and that she has a clear right to the Commissioner’s performance of that duty.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court found the appellant failed to meet the mandamus test requiring a public legal duty and clear right.

propositions.text: The appellant cites RCMP Act s.5(1) as source of Commissioner's duty to respond and investigate misconduct allegations.
propositions.quote: The appellant cites subsection 5(1) of the RCMP Act, which grants the Commissioner the responsibility and authority for the management and control of the RCMP, as the source of the legal right to have the Commissioner respond to her questions and investigate the allegations ...

propositions.text: The appellant contends a public legal duty arises from common law police duties described in R. v. Godoy.
propositions.quote: The appellant also contends that a public legal duty to act arises from the common law duties of police as described by the Supreme Court in R. v. Godoy, such as preservation of the peace, the prevention of crime and the protection of life and property ...

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RCMP Act and common law police duties create a public legal duty to respond and investigate misconduct allegations.

propositions.text: These arguments fail.
propositions.quote: These arguments fail.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that these arguments fail.

propositions.text: Subsection 5(1) grants the Commissioner authority for RCMP management and control.
propositions.quote: Subsection 5(1) is the source of the Commissioner’s authority for the management and control of the RCMP.

propositions.text: Statutory authority to a public official does not create a legal right for citizens to demand exercise of discretion in a certain way absent effect on legal rights.
propositions.quote: Absent an effect on a legally cognizable right or interest, a grant of statutory authority to a public official does not give rise to a legal right on the part of a citizen to require that the associated administrative discretion of management and control be exercised in a certain way, or at all (see, for example, Reisdorf v. Canada, 2023 FCA 188 at para. 8).

propositions.text: The Commissioner had no legal obligation to respond within the unilateral, arbitrary and extremely short deadline imposed in the June 19th email.
propositions.quote: the Commissioner had no legal obligation to respond within the unilateral, arbitrary and extremely short deadline” imposed in the June 19th email (Federal Court Decision, at para. 27).

propositions.text: There is no error in the Federal Court’s finding about the Commissioner’s lack of legal obligation to respond within the deadline.
propositions.quote: There is therefore no error in the Federal Court’s finding that “the Commissioner had no legal obligation to respond within the unilateral, arbitrary and extremely short deadline” imposed in the June 19th email (Federal Court Decision, at para. 27).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains subsection 5(1) grants the Commissioner authority, no legal right arises for citizens to demand discretion exercise, and finds no error in the Federal Court's ruling on the Commissioner's obligation.

propositions.text: The appellant relies on common law duties of the police to support her position.
propositions.quote: The appellant’s reliance on the common law duties of the police does not assist her position.

propositions.text: Common law duties of police do not create a positive duty for the Commissioner to respond to the appellant's email.
propositions.quote: Whatever the scope of those duties, they do not translate into a positive duty on the part of the Commissioner to respond to the appellant's email.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues common law police duties support her, but the court finds no positive duty to respond arises from those duties.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed with costs fixed at $2,500.
propositions.quote: The appeal will therefore be dismissed with costs which I would fix in the all-inclusive amount of $2,500.

propositions.text: Judges Rennie, Gleason, and Locke agree with the dismissal and costs order.
propositions.quote: “Donald J. Rennie” J.A. “I agree. Mary J.L. Gleason J.A.” “I agree. George R. Locke J.A.”

propositions.text: The hearing took place in Calgary, Alberta on October 22, 2025.
propositions.quote: PLACE OF HEARING: CALGARY, ALBERTA DATE OF HEARING: october 22, 2025

propositions.text: The judgment was dated November 20, 2025.
propositions.quote: DATED: NOVEMBER 20, 2025

propositions.text: The appellant is Caroline O’Driscoll appearing on her own behalf.
propositions.quote: Caroline O’Driscoll ON HER OWN BEHALF

propositions.text: The respondents are Royal Canadian Mounted Police Commissioner Michael Duheme and Attorney General of Canada, represented by counsel and solicitors.
propositions.quote: For The Respondents ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE COMMISSIONER MICHAEL DUHEME and ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA SOLICITORS OF RECORD: Shalene Curtis-Micallef Deputy Attorney General of Canada For The Respondents ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE COMMISSIONER MICHAEL DUHEME and ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal with costs of $2,500; judges concur; hearing and parties' details are noted.
